review: The hymn is the church's warfare: 1:1 is Rev 22:7 with 1 Pet 5:8, 1:2–3 Eph 6:10–11 (הִתְחַזְּרוּ בִּכְלֵי נֶשֶׁק), 2:2–4 1 Pet 5:8 (כְּאַרְיֵה שֹׁאֵג) with Job 1:7, 3:3 the armour of Eph 6:14–17, and 4:4–5 the Captain of Zech 14:3 and Rev 19:11.

2:1 שָׁלַף צוֹרֵר הַנֶּפֶשׁ — the Arabic إِنَّ خَصْمَ النَّفْسِ يَشْهَر صَارِمَ الْقِتَال puts the drawing and the sword in two lines; the Hebrew follows the same enjambment, so the sword does not appear until the second line, which is how the print builds the threat.

3:1 אֹיְבֵי הַצֶּדֶק — the plural construct is deliberate: the Arabic أَعْدَاءَ الصَّلَاحِ is 'the foes of righteousness', and the Hebrew keeps the abstract הַצֶּדֶק rather than a moral adjective, so the stanza's enemy is a power and not merely wicked men.

4:1 תִּבְעַר מִלְחַמְתֵּנוּ — the Arabic حَرْبُنَا الْعُظْمَى تَشُبُّ is 'our great war flames up'; the Hebrew keeps בָּעַר (Exod 3:2, בֹּעֵר בָּאֵשׁ) as the verb of the flame and puts the greatness into the noun, so the line still reads as one clause.

5:3–4 אֵיךְ נִירָא מִתְּבוּסָה … תְּשׁוּעָתֵנוּ גְּלוּיָה — the Arabic's rhetorical question is kept as a question, because the stanza's force is the absurdity of fear, not a statement of courage; תְּבוּסָה is post-biblical for 'defeat', used because biblical Hebrew has no single noun for it and the line needs the abstract.
